newsitem.title: USA: U.S. study finds "family TV" full of sex.
newsitem.headline: U.S. study finds "family TV" full of sex.

text.p: Children who watch television are being inundated with sexual material even from the "family hour" programs commonly believed to be free of adult topics, a study released on Wednesday found.

Three out of four shows the major networks air during the so-called family hour contain some sexual content, and a typical hour contains eight sexual messages, according to the study by the Kaiser Family Foundation and the children's policy group Children Now.
The family hour was conceived in the 1970s as the time between 8 and 9 p.m. when families could sit together and watch television free of offensive or risque material.

But over the past 20 years, sexual content in that time slot has risen more than four-fold, the study found. It defined sexual material as scenes showing sexual activity as well as discussion or suggestion of it.

Even when the sexual message was only innuendo, children were often found to understand. "Children as young as eight understood a reference to whipped cream in the bedroom, and others understood veiled references to male anatomy and jokes about virginity," the study said.

Moreover, their basis for understanding often was another television show. Asked whether she thought it was realistic that the male and female characters in the NBC hit "Friends" talked about sex in public, one pre-teen girl interviewed for the study said it was. Her reasoning: "I've seen that on "Seinfeld," referring to another NBC sitcom.

The study did not say all the sexual material airing was inappropriate for young viewers. Children responded that the shows they liked best were those that addressed the risks or responsibilities related to sex.
Yet it found those episodes were rare. Fewer than one in 10 scenes of a sexual nature included any mention of uplanned pregnancy, sexually transmitted disease or birth control.

"We're not in a position of saying this is good or bad," said Matt James, a spokesman for the Kaiser Family Foundation. "But the thing that jumped out at me is the sheer fact that sexual content has doubled over every 10 year period, and yet there are not that many more socially responsible messages."

Networks at one time embraced the concept of a family hour as a way to attract viewers, but drifted away from it as households began acquiring a second or third television and children began watching television apart from their parents.

Some networks, now airing some of their raciest material at 8 p.m., no longer make any pretensions of offering family programming. The study found parents were often surprised by the adult content of material on TV so early in the evening.
